query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Engineering a hierarchical microstructure that features nano-scale disordered FCC particles dispersed within ordered L12 precipitates in a high-entropy alloy will improve its mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance relative to a conventional homogeneous microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a conventional, relatively homogeneous microstructure (e.g., single-phase FCC or dual-phase without intentional hierarchical dispersion).
generation.intervention: Tailor alloy composition and heat treatment to induce in-situ formation of a hierarchical microstructure containing nano-scale FCC particles embedded within ordered L12 precipitates in an FCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature under loading conditions typical for aerospace fasteners, with corrosion evaluations in a saline environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a hierarchical dispersion of nano-FCC particles within L12 precipitate islands embedded in the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Nano-scale FCC particles serve as obstacles to dislocation movement and grain-boundary sliding, enhancing mechanical durability and creep resistance. The ordered L12 precipitates contribute to microstructural stability and reduce preferential pathways for corrosion, thereby enhancing overall corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline, the engineered alloy is expected to exhibit increased yield strength, reduced room-temperature creep strain rates, and lower corrosion current densities, indicating improved mechanical and corrosion properties suitable for aerospace fasteners.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy processed without the hierarchical microstructure intervention.
generation.boundary: The improvements are anticipated under room-temperature conditions and for high-entropy alloy compositions amenable to forming the desired hierarchical phases; the effect may not extend to alloys operating under extreme temperature regimes or markedly different compositions.
generation.uncertainty: While prior work supports the beneficial role of hierarchical microstructures in high-entropy superalloys, the precise magnitude of improvements in durability, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance remains uncertain until validated by dedicated testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy fastener samples: one set processed conventionally and one set processed to develop the targeted hierarchical microstructure via controlled alloying and heat treatment. Perform standardized mechanical testing (tensile and creep tests) at room temperature and conduct corrosion tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution. Use TEM to verify the microstructural differences.
measurements: Corrosion current density and pitting characteristics
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of the microstructure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hierarchical microstructure samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in yield strength, lower creep strain rates, and enhanced corrosion resistance (e.g., reduced corrosion current density) compared to the conventionally processed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

AbstractA hierarchical microstructure strengthened high entropy superalloy (HESA) with superior cost specific yield strength from room temperature up to 1,023 K is presented. By phase transformation pathway through metastability, HESA possesses a hierarchical microstructure containing a dispersion of nano size disordered FCC particles inside ordered L12 precipitates that are within the FCC matrix. The average tensile yield strength of HESA from room temperature to 1,023 K could be 120 MPa higher than that of advanced single crystal superalloy, while HESA could still exhibit an elongation greater than 20%. Furthermore, the cost specific yield strength of HESA can be 8 times that of some superalloys. A template for lighter, stronger, cheaper, and more ductile high temperature alloy is proposed.Subject terms: Mechanical properties, Metals and alloys

Hierarchical HESA has shown outstanding high temperature tensile properties in this work. Creep resistance is also an important property for high temperature application. Although the disappearance of FCC particles at 1,023 K after 200 h, Fig. 3c, suggested that HESA would have to rely on remaining L12 precipitates for strengthening, our previous work has shown that without nano FCC particles, HESA possessed similar creep resistance as that of CMSX-2. The future challenge would be to prolong the thermal stability of FCC particles inside L12 phase, this might be the future direction to develop more creep resistant HESA. Alloy design may utilize more slow diffusing species such as Mo to improve the stability of hierarchical microstructure, and CALPHAD method will need to be utilized for alloy design to avoid formation of detrimental topologically close-packed (TCP) phases,.

chosen.approach: Design hierarchical microstructure in high‐entropy superalloys
